why_how.text: Signals organize movement for both groups at the stated locations. Their function should not be reduced to only one road-user type.
A dead signal uses the stated stop-sign-style procedure. First arrival still requires caution rather than a forced movement.
The source tells pedestrians to obey their dedicated signals when present. A vehicle’s green does not replace a contrary pedestrian instruction.
The source distinguishes starting from continuing an existing crossing. A change in display is not an instruction to freeze in the crosswalk.
The permission retains stopping, the applicable prohibition and yielding conditions. It is not a general right to turn without checking.
The left-on-red provision has a one-way-to-one-way condition. Do not import the broader right-turn permission into every left turn.
The source expressly retains the allowed-turns-on-red exception while requiring a stop. Neither unconditional movement nor deletion of the exception preserves the statement.
Flashing red uses a stop-sign-style response. The completed stop does not erase the subsequent observation and yielding.
The source limits entry against steady yellow to being too close to stop safely. Pedestrians separately retain any instruction from their pedestrian signal.
This arrow concerns the end of the protected interval, not the same situation as a flashing yellow arrow.
The source describes an unprotected opportunity. The flashing arrow permits the turn only with the stated yielding and gap conditions.
Flashing yellow has a caution meaning. It should not be confused with flashing red or a protected green arrow.
Green permits cautious movement rather than guaranteeing that every other road user complies. Turning protection is a separate signal distinction.
The source distinguishes permission to move from protection of the indicated turn. Retain the oncoming-traffic and pedestrian duties for the unprotected movement.
The source contrasts stopping procedures with a caution display. Do not transfer flashing yellow’s response to a dead or flashing-red signal.
The dedicated pedestrian display governs the walker in this situation. Vehicle permission does not override it.
The permissions are conditional and have different street-direction scope. Keep the shared stopping requirement and the specific left-turn condition.
The source expressly preserves the red-arrow exception. The flashing-red procedure still requires stopping, yielding and a safe opportunity.
The arrow’s behavior changes its meaning. The source’s unprotected flashing-yellow turn retains oncoming and pedestrian duties.
The displays differ, but neither promises that all other road users comply. The source keeps caution with movement.
Permission to move and protection of a particular turn are different. The source expressly preserves yielding for the unprotected turn.

scenario.text: A learner faces this decision: How should an intersection signal that is not working be treated?

reasoning.text: The proposed response is “Like an unconditional green signal for every approach.”. That alternative does not preserve the stated rule. A signal that is not working is treated like stop signs in every direction, with the driver who stops first going first while staying cautious.

result.text: Choose “Like stop signs in every direction, with the first driver to stop proceeding first while remaining cautious.”. Keep the setting and every stated condition attached to that response.

claim.text: Common mistake: “Like an unconditional green signal for every approach.”.

correction.text: A signal that is not working is treated like stop signs in every direction, with the driver who stops first going first while staying cautious.

memory_support.text: Remember “Pedestrian and vehicle signals”. Connect the person or setting to the required action, then check the full statement for limits or exceptions.

prompt.text: Consider the earlier decision. Is “Like an unconditional green signal for every approach.” a sound response? Give the correction and explain the condition that decides it.

answer.text: A signal that is not working is treated like stop signs in every direction, with the driver who stops first going first while staying cautious.

rationale.text: The correction follows the stated rule rather than the proposed alternative. A signal that is not working is treated like stop signs in every direction, with the driver who stops first going first while staying cautious.

lines.text: A dead signal is not an assumed green or flashing-yellow display.

narration.text: Traffic signals organize movement for vehicles and pedestrians at the locations described in the handbook. Their presence does not replace the need to understand the particular display or road user. A signal that is not working is treated using the stated stop-sign-style approach, with first stop going first while remaining cautious. Do not substitute a remembered green display or flashing-yellow response for a dead signal. The absence of a working display creates the described stopping procedure rather than a situation in which every approach can proceed without yielding.

title.text: Keep the pedestrian display in view

lines.text: Starting and finishing a crossing are different situations.
Pedestrians use their dedicated displays when those signals are present.

narration.text: Pedestrians use their dedicated displays when those signals are present. WALK permits starting from the curb or sidewalk, while DON’T WALK tells someone still waiting not to begin. A person already crossing when the display begins flashing continues across rather than freezing in the crosswalk. The vehicle light does not override that pedestrian instruction. The source also preserves this priority when describing a pedestrian facing yellow: do not start unless a pedestrian signal directs otherwise. Keep starting, continuing and following the dedicated display distinct.

lines.text: The source’s red-arrow exception still includes the required stop.
A red-light turn is conditional, not a movement without a stop.

narration.text: A red-light turn is conditional, not a movement without a stop. The handbook gives the stopping position, preserves signs or officer directions that prohibit the turn, and retains yielding to pedestrians, bicycles and traffic. It limits the described left turn on red to one-way street onto one-way street. For a steady red arrow, the source explicitly says to remain stopped except for the allowed turns on red. Keep that exception rather than erase it, but do not broaden it into a protected turn or assume that a signal alone establishes a safe path.

lines.text: A caution display and a stop-sign-style display are different instructions.
Flashing red and flashing yellow call for different responses.

narration.text: Flashing red and flashing yellow call for different responses. Flashing red uses a complete stop, observation, yielding and safe movement, like the described stop-sign procedure. Flashing yellow calls for cautious movement and usually slowing, rather than the same automatic full-stop response. Neither display guarantees that conflicts are absent. A learner who recognizes only the color but ignores whether the light flashes can select the wrong procedure. Read the whole display and keep the resulting stop or caution instruction with its remaining observation and yielding conditions.

lines.text: Steady and flashing arrows do not offer the same turning condition.
Yellow displays also need their full form.

narration.text: Yellow displays also need their full form. A steady yellow vehicle light warns that red is next and restricts entry to the too-close-to-stop-safely situation. A steady yellow arrow ends the protected-turn interval, so vehicles completing the turn clear and prepare for the next display. A flashing yellow arrow instead permits an unprotected left turn with yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians and a safe gap. These are not interchangeable yellow permissions. Keep the dedicated pedestrian-signal override as well rather than turn a vehicle-light sentence into an exceptionless instruction for every walker.

lines.text: A plain green is not automatically a protected turning arrow.

narration.text: A steady green allows cautious movement, including attention to traffic that may run red. A green arrow identifies protection for the indicated turn, while a turning vehicle without that arrow remains unprotected and yields to oncoming traffic and pedestrians as stated. Keep movement permission separate from turning protection. A plain green does not establish that an approaching vehicle will comply, and it is not automatically a protected arrow for every maneuver. The source therefore preserves observation even where a display permits movement and identifies particular yielding for the unprotected turn.

lines.text: A dead-signal response includes stopping and a safe opportunity.

narration.text: A driver arrives first at an intersection whose signal is not working and assumes that being first removes the need to stop or look. What does the handbook actually keep? The dead-signal procedure is stop-sign style, with first stop going first while remaining cautious. The completed stop and safe opportunity still matter. The example is not answered by borrowing flashing yellow’s caution-only response or by remembering a green light from an earlier trip. Identify the current nonworking signal and use the stated procedure rather than treating arrival order as unconditional permission.

lines.text: A color alone does not identify every condition for every road user.

narration.text: For recall, read who the display addresses, its color, its shape and whether it is steady or flashing. Those features distinguish pedestrian instructions, red-turn conditions, stop-sign-style flashing red, caution-only flashing yellow and the different arrow meanings. Then retain the remaining yielding and observation. This approach keeps a simple color slogan from erasing a qualifier, such as a pedestrian-signal override or the allowed-turns-on-red exception. The source gives specific displays and conditions, not a promise that every green, yellow or red situation has one identical response for every road user.

why_how.text: The source connects the low operating speed with slowing on approach. Preparation should occur before entering the circulating space.
The entering driver yields to the traffic already inside. Direction and priority should not be borrowed from an all-way stop.
The source prohibits an in-circle pass in the single-lane situation. Clear movement in the lane is different from overtaking another vehicle.
The right signal communicates the exit, but the pedestrian yielding condition remains. Announcing the movement is not the same as clearing its path.
The apron accommodates the described large-vehicle wheel path. It is not extra passing space for a smaller vehicle.
The source retains marked crossings and caution. A vehicle’s yielding duty does not turn the central island into the pedestrian route.
The source describes a walking option and a vehicle-riding option. It does not direct riders to the island or replace clear signaling.
The source distinguishes clearing the roundabout from pulling over afterward. A pre-entry pull-over is conditional on available room.
The roundabout uses the already-circulating priority described by the source, not a first-arrived contest at the entrance.
The source gives the roundabout its own prohibition without replacing the ordinary passing rules everywhere else.
The source calls for clearing the roundabout rather than creating a stop inside it.

scenario.text: A learner faces this decision: Who has priority when a driver enters a roundabout?

reasoning.text: The proposed response is “Only the vehicle entering at the highest speed.”. That alternative does not preserve the stated rule. Yield to vehicles already inside the roundabout because they hold the right-of-way, and remember that circulation runs counterclockwise.

result.text: Choose “Vehicles already circulating inside it.”. Keep the setting and every stated condition attached to that response.

claim.text: Common mistake: “Only the vehicle entering at the highest speed.”.

correction.text: Yield to vehicles already inside the roundabout because they hold the right-of-way, and remember that circulation runs counterclockwise.

memory_support.text: Remember “Roundabouts”. Connect the person or setting to the required action, then check the full statement for limits or exceptions.

prompt.text: Consider the earlier decision. Is “Only the vehicle entering at the highest speed.” a sound response? Give the correction and explain the condition that decides it.

answer.text: Yield to vehicles already inside the roundabout because they hold the right-of-way, and remember that circulation runs counterclockwise.

rationale.text: The correction follows the stated rule rather than the proposed alternative. Yield to vehicles already inside the roundabout because they hold the right-of-way, and remember that circulation runs counterclockwise.

lines.text: The entrant does not gain priority by reaching the approach first.

narration.text: Roundabout preparation begins with slowing on approach and yielding to vehicles already circulating. The handbook describes counterclockwise movement and gives that circulating traffic priority over an entrant. An empty approach line is not itself a safe gap in the circle, and a signal does not make an entering vehicle the priority vehicle. Keep the approach speed, direction and existing traffic in the same decision rather than focus only on reaching the entrance before another driver.

title.text: Keep entry and exit checks separate

lines.text: A clear entrance does not perform the later pedestrian check.
Enter to the right of the center island and continue when the way is clear.

narration.text: Enter to the right of the center island and continue when the way is clear. The handbook prohibits passing inside a single-lane roundabout, so a slower vehicle ahead is not an invitation to overtake within the circle. When the desired street is reached, signal right and yield to pedestrians in or waiting at the exit crosswalk. Entry, circulation and exit are connected but different tasks. A clear entry does not establish a clear exit later, and an exit signal communicates intention without removing the pedestrian check or turning the apron into a passing lane.

title.text: Use the intended route and space

lines.text: The truck apron and central island are not general shortcuts.
Different roundabout users need their appropriate space and route.

narration.text: Different roundabout users need their appropriate space and route. The handbook says large vehicles need room as rear wheels track over the truck apron, with smaller vehicles dropping behind. Pedestrians use marked crossings rather than walking to the center island and remain cautious. Bicyclists are offered a walking route on sidewalks and crosswalks or riding the circulating roadway as a vehicle with clear signals. Do not treat the apron as spare passing room or the center island as the crossing destination. The source describes those features for different purposes.

title.text: Clear the circle before pulling over

lines.text: The driver’s current position determines the described emergency response.

narration.text: An approaching emergency vehicle does not change the roundabout into a place to stop in the circulating lane. The handbook tells a driver already inside to exit normally and then pull right. Before entering, pulling over is conditional on having room. Keep the stage of the journey with the response: outside before entry and inside the circle are not the same position. Stopping immediately wherever the vehicle happens to be can overlook the specific instruction to clear the circle. The source’s sequence avoids replacing a stated response with a generic pull-over habit applied in the wrong place.

lines.text: Yield to vehicles already circulating inside the roundabout.

narration.text: An entering driver reaches the roundabout approach before a vehicle that is already circulating and claims first-arrival priority. What rule has been imported incorrectly? The handbook gives priority to vehicles inside the roundabout, with the entrant yielding. The driver still slows on approach and waits for a clear opportunity. This example tests the correct traffic relationship rather than who wants to enter first. A desired gap is not an actual gap, and a turn signal is not a transfer of priority from the circulating vehicle.

lines.text: Each stage retains its own space, priority and crossing conditions.

narration.text: Organize roundabout driving as approach, circulation and exit while remembering the other users. Approach slowly and yield to circulating traffic. Keep the single-lane no-passing rule and allow large vehicles the room described for their wheel path. At the exit, signal and check the pedestrian crossing. Preserve the marked pedestrian route, the bicycle choices and the emergency-vehicle sequence. This organization is a study aid for the distinct instructions, not permission to assume an earlier clear position means every later movement is clear or that a special road feature is an available shortcut.

why_how.text: The source keeps uncertainty, far-side space and gear changes in the crossing decision. A vehicle should not enter on the assumption that room will appear.
The source lists several stop triggers, not only a fully lowered gate or a train already across the road. The original minimum rail distance remains part of the provision.
Advance warning creates readiness for the crossing. It is not a guarantee about the track or an instruction to rush toward it.
These markings identify the approaching railroad-crossing situation. They are different from lane-use or parking markings.
The track-count information matters at multiple tracks. A crossbuck is not evidence that every track is clear.
Flashing itself triggers the stop. Multiple tracks add the need to check all of them rather than assume one cleared train settles the crossing.
The source retains both the raised-gate and ended-flashing conditions. A partially changed display is not the described release.
The source distinguishes preparing for a crossing from the active condition requiring a stop.
The release has both conditions. Physical space does not replace the ended-flashing instruction.

scenario.text: A learner faces this decision: Which railroad-crossing approach matches the stated precautions?

reasoning.text: The proposed response is “Race the train whenever the vehicle appears faster.”. That alternative does not preserve the stated rule. Never race a train to the crossing, stop whenever safety is in doubt, keep space for the vehicle on the far side, and avoid shifting gears on the tracks.

result.text: Choose “Do not race a train; stop if safety is doubtful and leave room beyond the tracks.”. Keep the setting and every stated condition attached to that response.

claim.text: Common mistake: “Race the train whenever the vehicle appears faster.”.

correction.text: Never race a train to the crossing, stop whenever safety is in doubt, keep space for the vehicle on the far side, and avoid shifting gears on the tracks.

memory_support.text: Remember “Railroad crossings”. Connect the person or setting to the required action, then check the full statement for limits or exceptions.

prompt.text: Consider the earlier decision. Is “Race the train whenever the vehicle appears faster.” a sound response? Give the correction and explain the condition that decides it.

answer.text: Never race a train to the crossing, stop whenever safety is in doubt, keep space for the vehicle on the far side, and avoid shifting gears on the tracks.

rationale.text: The correction follows the stated rule rather than the proposed alternative. Never race a train to the crossing, stop whenever safety is in doubt, keep space for the vehicle on the far side, and avoid shifting gears on the tracks.

lines.text: Reaching the rails is not the same as having room to clear them.

narration.text: Railroad-crossing readiness includes what happens beyond the first rail. The handbook warns against racing a train, calls for a stop whenever safety is doubtful, requires room for the vehicle on the far side and advises against changing gears on the tracks. A driver should not enter on the assumption that blocked space will become available. The crossing decision is not simply whether the front of the vehicle can reach the rails first. Keep the whole vehicle’s passage and the safe stopping decision together rather than use speed or urgency to replace a clear route through the crossing.

lines.text: A fully lowered gate is not the only condition requiring a stop.
The handbook lists several conditions that require stopping: crossing controls and warnings, a watchman and
the specified approaching-train or hazardous-train situations.

narration.text: The handbook lists several conditions that require stopping: crossing controls and warnings, a watchman and the specified approaching-train or hazardous-train situations. The stop also retains the source’s minimum distance from the nearest rail. Do not narrow the rule to a gate that has already fallen or a train that has already occupied the road. Flashing lights trigger a stop when they begin, and multiple tracks require checking every track before proceeding later. One visible train or one partly changed control does not establish that the whole crossing is clear.

lines.text: A crossing warning is not evidence that every track is clear.
Different crossing warnings give different information.

narration.text: Different crossing warnings give different information. An advance sign calls for slowing, looking, listening and readiness to stop at the crossing ahead. Pavement markings with the described line, cross and letters identify the crossing approach. A crossbuck marks the public crossing, and an additional sign can state that more than one track exists. These are not promises that the tracks are clear. Keep advance readiness separate from an active flashing or gate condition that requires the stop, and keep any track-count information in the later observation before crossing.

lines.text: A moving gate and ended flashing are not interchangeable conditions.

narration.text: At a gated crossing, the stop begins when the lights flash rather than waiting until the gate physically falls. The handbook says to remain stopped until the gates rise and the flashing ends. Both conditions matter. A rising gate does not by itself end active flashing, and physical space around or beneath a barrier is not the described permission to proceed. Where several tracks exist, the driver also checks that every track is clear. Keep the control’s completed release with the actual crossing view instead of treating the departure of one train as the entire decision.

title.text: A clear first rail is insufficient

lines.text: The vehicle needs room beyond the crossing before entering it.

narration.text: A driver sees no train but cannot fit beyond the crossing because traffic ahead has stopped. Is reaching the crossing before a train enough? The handbook says to leave room for the vehicle on the far side and stop whenever safety is doubtful. The empty-looking first track does not solve the blocked exit. This example tests the whole crossing path rather than a race to a particular point. It also preserves the warning against shifting gears on the tracks: the crossing should not be planned around stopping there to select a different gear or wait for traffic to make room.

lines.text: One changed condition does not establish that the complete crossing is ready.

narration.text: For recall, separate warning, stopping and clearance. Advance signs, markings and crossbucks identify the approach and the need for readiness. The listed active controls or train conditions require the stated stop. Gates and flashing retain their complete-release conditions, and multiple tracks need every-track observation. The path beyond the rails still needs enough room for the vehicle. This structure prevents one favorable observation, such as a departing train or a partly rising gate, from being used as proof that every other control and space condition has already been satisfied.

why_how.text: The broken-yellow description concerns a passing situation. Keep line color, pattern and the separate safe-passing conditions in view.
The source distinguishes passing from the stated left-turn maneuver. Neither deleting nor broadening the exception preserves it.
Color identifies the traffic relationship in the source. Solid edge lines have a separate road-edge role.
The source keeps the lane-change opportunity and the stronger stay-in-lane instruction distinct. A dashed line does not guarantee a clear adjacent lane.
The stopping position protects the crossing area. The source also retains pedestrian duties when a crosswalk is not marked.
The driver’s side of the pair determines the passing permission. The source separately bars passing across two solid yellow lines.
The source permits the described left turn when safe. It is not general passing permission.
A reversible lane changes allowed direction with time. Its previous use does not establish its current permission.
The source distinguishes steady yellow’s changing-use instruction from flashing yellow’s turning-only meaning and green’s permitted use.
The sign defines the reservation. A marking should not be read as canceling the special-use condition it accompanies.
The source ties eligibility to occupancy and the posted schedule. A general lane preference does not meet those conditions.
The lane is shared for the described turning uses, not general through travel or passing. Its use does not mean conflicting movements may be forced.
The absence of a special control does not remove the general road rules.
The source uses line color to identify the traffic pattern. The color is information about lane relationships rather than a decoration.
The driver’s side controls the described permission. Reading only the existence of any dashed paint loses that condition.
The markings have different functions while the pedestrian yielding instruction remains. The source also warns that not every crosswalk is marked.
The two controls answer different questions: who may use the lane and which direction is currently allowed.
Shared turning access is not unrestricted through use or permission for conflicting simultaneous movements. The reversible lane keeps its current-direction condition.
The source gives distinct meanings to flashing and steady yellow. Keep the turn-only instruction separate from the changing-use instruction.

scenario.text: A learner faces this decision: Under the stated centerline rule, when may a broken yellow centerline be crossed?

reasoning.text: The proposed response is “To travel indefinitely against traffic.”. That alternative does not preserve the stated rule. A broken yellow centerline may be crossed, but only to overtake or pass another vehicle.

result.text: Choose “To overtake or pass another vehicle.”. Keep the setting and every stated condition attached to that response.

claim.text: Common mistake: “To travel indefinitely against traffic.”.

correction.text: A broken yellow centerline may be crossed, but only to overtake or pass another vehicle.

memory_support.text: Remember “Roadway markings and lanes”. Connect the person or setting to the required action, then check the full statement for limits or exceptions.

prompt.text: Consider the earlier decision. Is “To travel indefinitely against traffic.” a sound response? Give the correction and explain the condition that decides it.

answer.text: A broken yellow centerline may be crossed, but only to overtake or pass another vehicle.

rationale.text: The correction follows the stated rule rather than the proposed alternative. A broken yellow centerline may be crossed, but only to overtake or pass another vehicle.

lines.text: A line’s appearance does not guarantee a clear neighboring lane.

narration.text: Road markings identify traffic relationships as well as permissions. The handbook uses white between lanes traveling the same direction and yellow between opposing traffic, while solid edge lines show the road edge. For same-direction lanes, dashed white allows a safe lane change and solid white says to remain in lane except for the stated special situation. Keep color and pattern together rather than read either alone as every answer. A dashed line does not promise an empty adjacent lane, and an edge line does not become an opposing-traffic centerline merely because it is painted on the road.

lines.text: A left-turn exception is not general permission to overtake.
Yellow passing markings depend on the pattern and the driver’s side.

narration.text: Yellow passing markings depend on the pattern and the driver’s side. The source describes a dashed line as permitting a safe pass, a solid-plus-dashed pair as permitting passing only from the dashed side, and two solid lines as barring passing in both directions. It separately retains a safe left-turn exception across a solid line into the listed destinations. Keep passing and turning distinct. A left-turn exception does not create unrestricted overtaking permission, while the passing prohibition should not be used to erase the expressly described left-turn maneuver.

title.text: Keep the stop before the crossing

lines.text: A missing painted crosswalk does not establish that no pedestrian duty exists.
A stop line locates the vehicle’s required halt, while a crosswalk identifies the pedestrian crossing
area.

narration.text: A stop line locates the vehicle’s required halt, while a crosswalk identifies the pedestrian crossing area. The handbook says to stop before reaching the relevant line or crosswalk and yield to pedestrians in or about to enter the crossing. It also warns that not all crosswalks are marked. Do not treat a missing painted crossing as proof that there is no pedestrian duty, or use a visible crosswalk as the place to leave the vehicle blocking the way. Position and yielding are connected parts of the stop, not choices between obeying a signal and considering the person crossing.

lines.text: Previous use does not establish the reversible lane’s current permission.
A reversible lane changes the direction it carries at different times, so the driver checks
the current signs or overhead displays before entering.

narration.text: A reversible lane changes the direction it carries at different times, so the driver checks the current signs or overhead displays before entering. The handbook distinguishes a green arrow permitting use, a red X forbidding it, flashing yellow for turning only and steady yellow for leaving as soon as safely possible. The last two yellow displays are not interchangeable. A direction used yesterday does not establish permission now, and a lane wide enough for the vehicle is not evidence that it is currently open to that direction or to unrestricted through movement.

lines.text: Eligible use and current travel direction are different questions.
A reserved lane asks a different question from a reversible lane.

narration.text: A reserved lane asks a different question from a reversible lane. The sign identifies the special use or vehicle category, often accompanied by a white diamond. The handbook describes bus and bicycle reservations and occupancy conditions for high-occupancy lanes, including the signed minimum and posted days and hours. Read those signs rather than assume the diamond permits every vehicle. A reversible lane concerns current direction; a reservation concerns eligible use. Meeting an occupancy condition does not automatically answer a different lane’s direction control or replace the posted schedule.

lines.text: Shared access does not mean unrestricted or conflicting through travel.

narration.text: The shared center lane serves the source’s left-turn movements from either direction and permitted turn-arounds, not ordinary through travel or passing. The fact that both directions can use the turning lane does not authorize forcing conflicting simultaneous movements. Keep that purpose distinct from a reversible through lane, whose direction is controlled at the relevant time. Where signs and markings do not specify lane use, the general driving, passing and turning rules still apply. Absence of a special marking is not an absence of rules, just as a shared turning purpose is not unrestricted travel permission.

title.text: Permission is not a traffic gap

lines.text: A marking allowance does not establish a safe passing opportunity.

narration.text: A driver sees a broken yellow line and assumes it guarantees a safe pass regardless of oncoming traffic. What is missing? The handbook’s marking permission remains tied to safe passing. The driver’s side of a solid-plus-dashed pair also matters, and a separate left-turn exception must not be mistaken for passing permission. Read the intended maneuver and the actual pattern together. This example tests whether a permitted kind of movement has been confused with proof of a safe opportunity. Paint can describe an allowance without showing that the needed traffic gap currently exists.

title.text: Identify the question a control answers

lines.text: Direction, eligibility, turning purpose and a safe opportunity are different matters.

narration.text: For recall, ask what the marking or lane control is answering. Color can identify same or opposing traffic, while pattern describes lane changing or passing. Stop lines and crosswalks concern stopping position and pedestrians. Reversible controls identify current direction, reserved-lane signs identify eligible use, and shared-center markings identify the stated turning purpose. Keep these questions distinct instead of let one familiar symbol answer them all. The source’s general driving rules remain relevant where no special marking controls the lane, and every described permission keeps its own safety and condition limits.
